Autonomous agentic machine learning for biology

Agentomics

An agentic system that autonomously develops novel state-of-the-art solutions for biomedical machine learning tasks

Vlastimil Martinek, Andrea Gariboldi, Dimosthenis Tzimotoudis, Mark Galea, Elissavet Zacharopoulou, Aitor Alberdi Escudero, Edward Blake, David Čechák, Luke Cassar, Alessandro Balestrucci, Panagiotis Alexiou

University of Malta
  • Agentomics: an LLM agent system that takes a biomedical dataset and returns a trained, reusable ML model.
  • Published in Bioinformatics 42 (ISMB 2026 proceedings), doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag250. BioGeMT group, University of Malta, with CEITEC Masaryk University.

  • A typical cycle in a biology lab: question → ML task → data → model → evaluation, and back to a new question.
  • [click] time per step
  • Most steps take hours or days. Building a good ML model for a new biological dataset takes months: data representation, architecture, training, debugging, evaluation.
  • [click] co-scientist tools
  • Co-scientist AI tools try to automate the whole cycle. Their output (a hypothesis, an interpretation) is hard to score objectively.
  • [click] Agentomics
  • Agentomics targets one step: ML model development. It is the slowest step, and it is measurable: a model either scores well on held-out test data or it does not. Goal: months → hours.

AIDE · MLAgentBench

+write, run and fix code in a loop
−below human experts on biomedical ML benchmarks

  • AutoML (Auto-sklearn, AutoGluon, H2O) automates model selection and hyperparameter search, on pre-defined data representations. Biological data often needs domain-aware representations, custom deep networks or foundation models.
  • [click] LLM-written code
  • LLMs can write custom code, but without an error-correction loop a person has to run, debug and fix it (low success rate, SWE-bench).
  • [click] LLM agents
  • LLM agents add tools and a loop: write code, run it, read the error, fix it. AIDE and MLAgentBench are general ML agents; STELLA and Biomni are biomedical agents.
  • On BioML-bench they still fall below human expert models. Agents that execute code without isolation are a security risk, can see test labels, and can report metrics that no code computed.

  • The challenge we set ourselves. Given a well-defined ML task and a benchmark dataset with fixed training and test samples.
  • Produce a model that generalizes to the test set, code that retrains it and predicts on new data, and a record of what the agent did, with metrics.
  • [click]
  • Three requirements: fast, cheap, and correct. Correct means methodologically sound, reproducible, and with no test set leakage.

✓every step output is checked for structure and function, and the step is retried until it passes

✓an experiment design LLM plans each iteration from the results of all earlier iterations
  • When we used coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Aider) for ML on biological data, the same failures kept coming back. Grouped here in four rows.
  • [click] context
  • Long runs overflow the context and the agent forgets instructions. Agentomics splits the work into steps; each step is a new agent with a clean context, given only the short structured outputs of earlier steps. Tool output is capped at 5,000 characters.
  • [click] code
  • Scripts that do not run, outputs in a different format every time, success rate dropping as the run gets longer. Each step output must pass a structure check and a function check; if not, the agent gets the error and repeats the step.
  • [click] trust
  • Agents report metrics no code computed, touch test labels, delete files. In Agentomics the metrics come from our evaluation code, the test set is never visible to the agents, and everything runs in a Docker container with read-only mounts.
  • [click] strategy
  • Agents tend to polish one idea with small changes. A separate experiment design LLM reads all earlier iterations and plans the next one, with instructions to explore.

TEST METRICSadded to the report
hidden from the agents
  • Inputs: a training CSV with a label column; optionally a free-text description of the dataset (goes into the prompt) and a validation CSV (otherwise Agentomics splits one off). Classification and regression; DNA, RNA, protein and small-molecule data.
  • Everything runs in a Docker container with read-only mounts, so nothing on the host can be changed. The LLM is any supported provider, including local LLMs that keep sensitive data on the machine.
  • Agents act through 6 tools: bash, python write (checks syntax), python run, edit, foundation-model info (docs and code snippets) and final result (submits the step output as JSON). Pre-installed conda env with scikit-learn, torch, transformers.
  • 31 pre-downloaded foundation models across proteins, DNA, RNA and small molecules; more Hugging Face models can be added in a config file.
  • Outputs: a training script and an inference script with a fixed interface, the model files, the conda environment to run them, and a PDF report with the approach and metrics. Plus the full trace of agent actions.
  • [click] the test set
  • The test set is never mounted for the agents. After the run, our evaluation code runs the best iteration's inference script on it once and adds the test metrics to the report.

METRICSAgentomics runs inference.py
on train + validation splits
  • One iteration is seven fixed steps, always in this order. Each produces a structured output that summarises it for later steps.
  • [click] inside one step (training as the example)
  • Each step is a separate LLM agent with a clean context. Its prompt: base guidelines, the structured outputs of all earlier steps, and the instructions for this step. It uses the tools as often as it needs: explore, write files, run code, read the result.
  • It submits its result as JSON through the final result tool. The structure check requires valid JSON; the function check tests the step programmatically. If either fails, the agent gets the error message and must redo the same step. Over the retry limit, the iteration restarts from step 1.
  • [click] function check for training
  • For training: the script exists, takes the right arguments, runs again on a different subset of the data and produces the same artifacts as the submitted model. Data splitting: split files exist, columns kept, no sample in both splits. Inference: runs on a different subset and predicts every sample in the right format.
  • [click] metrics
  • After step 7, Agentomics itself runs the inference script on the train and validation splits and computes the metrics. No metric comes from the LLM.

  • A run repeats the seven-step iteration until a time or iteration limit. Each successful iteration produces one working model.
  • After each iteration, the step outputs and the train and validation metrics form an iteration summary. Before the next iteration, the experiment design LLM (high reasoning effort) reads the summaries of all completed iterations, the dataset description, available CPU and GPU, time left and the metric to optimise, and writes instructions for each step. Its prompt asks it to explore instead of making small incremental changes. Iterations share the file system, so later ones can reuse earlier models and scripts.
  • [click] budgets
  • Two run settings (values used in our benchmark). Baseline budget: the first 4 iterations use only simple models, to set a baseline. Split budget: during the first half of the run (4 of 8 h) the agent may re-split training and validation data. Only iterations on the latest split are compared, so the comparison stays fair.
  • [click] output
  • At the end, the output is the iteration with the best validation score, not the last one. Only then is the test set used: once, by our code, on that iteration's inference script.

   from published models
per dataset: 3 replicates × 8 h · NVIDIA RTX A4000 + 48 CPU cores · GPT-5.1-Codex-Max
test set hidden from the agents
leaderboard % = share of human leaderboard models that the agent's model beats on the test set
  • 20 established datasets with published state-of-the-art models, in three domains.
  • Protein engineering (ProteinGym, 6) and drug discovery (Polaris Hub, 9): we follow BioML-bench exactly, with the same evaluation criteria and time limits as the other agents. BioML-bench reports AIDE, MLAgentBench, STELLA and Biomni and a leaderboard of human expert models.
  • Regulatory genomics (Genomic Benchmarks and miRBench, 5): we ran Biomni ourselves with the same LLM, and built a human leaderboard by curating every published paper that reports test metrics on these datasets. The leaderboard is in the Agentomics repository.
  • Every dataset: 3 replicates of 8 h on one RTX A4000 and 48 CPU cores. GPT-5.1-Codex-Max for Agentomics, the zero-shot baseline (one LLM response) and our Biomni runs. The metric per dataset is the one used by the state of the art or by BioML-bench.
  • Score: leaderboard % is the share of human leaderboard models that the agent beats.
  • Leaderboard %: the share of human expert models beaten, mean ± SEM over successful runs (Table 1).
  • Agentomics is first in all three domains: 75.9 in protein engineering (next: AIDE 36.0), 34.3 in drug discovery (next: Biomni 32.6, AIDE 31.1), 60.2 in regulatory genomics (Biomni with the same LLM: 30.6).
  • Drug discovery is the hardest domain for every agent; the margin there is small.
  • Agentomics completed 100% of runs. AIDE completed 75% and 81%, STELLA 88% and 92%, the zero-shot LLM 56%, 48% and 80%. Failed runs are not in the leaderboard %, so agents that fail more are flattered.
  • Caveat: in protein engineering and drug discovery, the AIDE, MLAgentBench, STELLA and Biomni values are the ones reported by BioML-bench, with the LLMs used there. We ran Agentomics, the zero-shot baseline and the regulatory genomics Biomni runs ourselves, all with GPT-5.1-Codex-Max.

Agentomics, best of 3 worst to best of 3 human state of the art
  • Against the best published human model on each dataset (Table 2). We compare the best of 3 replicates; the bar shows the spread from worst to best replicate.
  • Protein engineering: new state of the art on 6 of 6. Regulatory genomics: 3 of 5, plus a tie on open chromatin (0.825 vs 0.825). Drug discovery: 2 of 9 (hERG, Caco-2). In total 11 of 20 datasets.
  • Counted per run instead of best-of-3: 19 of 60 runs beat the human state of the art. Replicates vary a lot on some datasets (SPIKE-SARS2: 0.25 to 0.93), so one 8-h run does not guarantee the best model.
  • Lipophilicity and Caco-2 use MAE: lower is better (arrow).
0.964
median correlation of validation and test scores
over the iterations of each run · the agent sees only the validation score
  • Agentomics picks models by validation score, so it could overfit the validation set. Check: correlation between validation score and hidden test score over all iterations of each run.
  • A: correlations per run. Median 0.964. Means: regulatory genomics 0.986, drug discovery 0.807, protein engineering 0.746. Optimising validation translates into test performance, so the validation splits Agentomics creates are representative.
  • B: best validation score so far, normalised per run (0 = worst iteration, 1 = best), averaged per domain over 8 h. It keeps rising.
  • C: the test score of the model that would be output at each time point. It rises too, with no dip late in the run. Drug discovery plateaus around 3 h: its best test scores came from iterations that were not best on validation.
364
iterations in the best run of each dataset; 20 output models
20%
of output models use foundation model embeddings; they rank higher on the leaderboards (P = 0.020)
drug discovery: no graph neural networks; weaker foundation models
  • Architectures in the best run of each of the 20 datasets: all 364 iterations (red) and the 20 output iterations (blue).
  • No single architecture dominates. Ensembles are the most common (XGBoost, random forests, custom ensembles), but the runs also built CNNs, transformers, SVMs, linear and logistic regression, and fine-tuned foundation models.
  • 20% of output models used foundation model embeddings, and those runs placed higher on the leaderboards (Mann–Whitney U, P = 0.020).
  • Weak spot: drug discovery. Its foundation-model iterations scored lower than in other domains, its validation–test correlations were lower, and no run built a graph neural network, which most drug discovery leaderboard models use.
  • Consequence: AutoML tools that search a fixed set of architectures and representations are not enough for biomedical ML.
AGO2 CLASH (Hejret 2023) · 8,193 miRNA–target pairs · do they bind?
0.880
AUPRC · best 8-h Agentomics run
0.860
best published model
  • Case study from our own field: AGO2 CLASH, 8,193 chimeric miRNA–target pairs. Each sample is two RNA sequences; the task is whether they bind in the context of AGO2. Many architectures have been tried on it (miRBench).
  • Best 8-h Agentomics run: AUPRC 0.880 on the test set, against 0.860 for the best published model.
  • [click] what the run did, in order
  • It started with logistic regression on one-hot RNA, then gradient-boosted trees, then CNNs and transformers.
  • Then it built interaction matrices of Watson–Crick and wobble pairs between miRNA and target, the representation that expert models use. This was not given to the agent.
  • It fine-tuned Nucleotide Transformer (~50M parameters), tried cross-attention dual encoders and CNN ensembles (residual, depthwise-separable, ConvNeXt-style), and several ensembling schemes.
  • The output: a probability-weighted combination of five ensembles built in five different iterations, the best on validation.

standards we propose for agentic ML
1
Sandboxruns in a container with restricted mounts
2
Hidden test setthe agent never sees the test data
3
Deterministic metricscomputed by evaluation code, not by the agent
4
Reusable outputsscripts that retrain the model and predict on new data
  • All 60 runs (20 datasets × 3) produced predictions, a valid conda environment, an inference script for new data and a training script that retrains on new data: 100% success.
  • Cost with GPT-5.1-Codex-Max (January 2026 prices): 9.4 ± 5.0 USD per 8-h run, 0.45 ± 0.09 USD per iteration. One iteration takes about 30 minutes (0.51 ± 0.32 h).
  • From this work we propose four standards for agentic ML systems: a sandbox to protect the user's machine and data; a test set strictly hidden from the agent; metrics computed by deterministic evaluation code; and reusable scripts and artifacts that others can inspect and rerun.
  • The risk is no longer that these systems fail to produce models; it is irreproducible code and inflated metrics from test set leakage.
  • Limitations: one LLM backbone, modest hardware, 8-h runs (some curves had not plateaued), 3 replicates, no ablation of components, CSV input only.

next data cycle: the agent assesses the job outputs
  • Agentomics starts from a dataset that someone has already collected and formatted. In the scientific cycle, the step before model development is data: an experiment or retrieval of public data, which takes days.
  • The experimental data module (ClosedLoop_AGML, in development) covers that step. From a short brief in plain words, with no human in the loop, it finds public data, builds a benchmark with a sealed test set, trains baseline models, runs Agentomics unmodified on the training and validation data, scores every model once on the test set and writes a report with 95% intervals. Code validators check every stage; an independent LLM reviewer checks the key stages.
  • A data agent searches the web, data repositories, papers and tool registries. It downloads public data that permit research use, and every file is recorded with its source URL and checksum.
  • When no processed release has the observations the task needs (for example interactions called from sequencing reads), the agent plans processing jobs: a published pipeline at a pinned version. A reviewer approves the plan, and the job runs offline in its own container. In the next data cycle the agent assesses the job outputs.
  • A reviewer with its own web search checks each decision. If no eligible public data exist, the run stops and states the reason.
  • A graphical interface for Agentomics that we are testing now. It shows a run as iterations and steps, with the duration and cost of each step.
  • A run on a breast cancer dataset. The left panel lists the iterations and their steps. The middle shows the plan the agent wrote for iteration 1, with instructions for each step. The right panel plots validation and train AUROC by iteration and lists the metrics of the selected iteration.
  • A run on a dataset of digit images. For each step the GUI lists the commands the agent ran and the files it wrote, then the step result. Here: the data exploration step of iteration 1.

  • Take-home: an agent that writes ML code can beat human expert models, if the system around it checks every step, computes metrics itself and never lets the agent see the test set.
  • Agentomics is open source and on PyPI: pip install agentomics. It guides the run set-up. No programming or ML expertise needed.
